To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) researchers’ decisions to adopt humanitarian identities can facilitate and constrain research; 2) humanitarian identities can undermine the insider status of local researchers; and 3) researchers’ use of humanitarian identities to facilitate access can lead to a “free-riding” problem, in which researchers benefit from the privileges and protections afforded to humanitarian staff without providing the services that are the basis for these privileges and protections.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the humanitarian identity is a powerful one, but it is not an all-encompassing or all-protecting one.
humanitarian affiliation in conflict-affected research is not an either/or proposition, but rather an ongoing negotiation of research identities that must be constantly renegotiated.
